latin.282: Subjungis hoc cogit nos fateri, primum illud Adami peccatum fuisse alio modo consideratum, & justo Dei judicio imputatum, & adscriptum toti naturae humanae. Mallem fateri meam ignorantiam: neque hujus confessionis me puderet: caecum enim esse arbitror qui non sentit se multo plura quam scit ignorare. Quam multa sunt in natura, quorum rationes cur sic fiant reddere nequimus? Satius mea sententia id esset, quam in Dei arcanam mentem irrumpentes, ei considerationem & judicium sine ulla revelatione tribuere, quod forte nec fuit, nec eum decet. Nosti enim illud Esai. 55. cogitationes meae non sunt ut cogitationes vestrae. Quam alti sunt coeli supra terram, tam altae sunt cogitationes meae supra cogitationes vestras: Et illud, quis novit mentem Domini?
latin.283: GAR. Hic vero inprimis ego quoque profiteor, malle me credere, hanc non esse affectatam ignorantiam, de qua dicunt illi apud Jobum cap. 21. 14. Recede a nobis, scientiam viarum tuarum nolumus, quam sinistram aliquam de Viro docto opinionem fovere. PLAC. Ecquam quaeso verbis illis sinistram de me opinionem fovendi ansam praebui, aut quid est in mea ista modesta & religiosa ignorantia, qua nolo sapere praeter Scripturam, simile abominandae illorum apud Jobum sceleratorum impietati?
latin.284: GAR. Miror solum, qua ratione ductus, eos arbitretur in arcanam Dei mentem irrumpere, qui corruptionis Originalis, & omnium poenarum in posteros ab ipsa nativitate incumbentium causam quaerunt in imputatione, adeoque participatione primi peccati; cum non ignoret veteres & Recentiores Theologos, hoc & docere, & profiteri se hausisse ex Apostoli doctrina Roman. v. Sicut postea frequentissimis testimoniis probabitur. Hos omnes gravissima accusatione urgere, quasi in arcanam Dei mentem temerario ausu irrumpentes, & limites illos transeuntes, quos Deus homini praestituit Deuter. XXIX. 29. nescio an fideciore satis consentaneum sit. PLAC. Primum agebatur de eo Dei actu interno, quo dicebatur Deus omnes homines considerasse tanquam unum hominem in Adamo. Idne veteres & Recentiores Theologi dixerunt? Idne colligi potest ex Apostoli doctrina Roman. v? Attulitne Vir doctus frequentissima testimonia ut id probaret? Tribuere Deo considerationem, actum quendam mentis & voluntatis internum praeter Scripturam, praeter rationem, quid est irrumpere in arcanam Dei mentem, si hoc non est?
latin.285: Idem, fateor, de immediata illa imputatione, in qua causa quaeritur originalis corruptionis, dici potest, si quidem ex sacris literis colligi nequit. Est enim ipsa quoque internus divinae mentis & voluntatis actus. Frustra me praejudiciis gravat; frustra Theologorum in me animos irritat: neque enim eos accuso, sed fraterne moneo, ut caveant sibi ab hoc scopulo. Humanum enim est errare, sed monitum in errore perseverare, turpe admodum, & periculosum est. Miror autem Theologos Reformatos talibus uti adversus fratres suos praejudiciis, quibus olim, & hoc tempore nihil veritati cognoscendae magis obstitit. Non enim quod hic, aut ille docuit, regula est fidei nostrae, sed id tantum, quod unicus noster doctor per suos Apostolos & Prophetas docuit. Illam autem imputationem neque Scriptura, neque plerique veteres Theologi, neque recentiores quidam agni nominis docuerunt: Et quosdam ipse contra se Vir doctus laudat. Exemplo sit Ludovicus Lavaterus insignis Theologus Tigurinus (unum enim attulisse exemplum sufficiet hoc loco) cujus haec verba ex Comm. in 2. Paralip. 25. citat cap. XVIII. pag. 629. Quisque scelerum suorum poenas luat. Hac lege Deus non obstringitur. Juste enim punit in omnibus hominibus peccatum primorum parentum, quod vitio originis sit cuique proprium. Quid potest magis opponi doctrinae Viri docti, passim affirmantis, peccatum primorum parentum nonnisi imputatione fieri nostrum?
latin.286: Quid si quaeram ex te rationem, cur primum illud Prorsus enim me fugit. Quanquam tu ultro nec rogatus videris reddere voluisse, addis enim haec verba, quia sc. Adam fuit primus homo, origo & stirps, seu radix omnium hominum. Agnosco, hinc intelligo potuisse una cum natura humana suum propagare vitium in posteros: at nego propterea ejus peccatum actuale nostrum fuisse, aut nobis debuisse imputari: nego inde considerationem illam & judicium, quod tu Deo tribuis, posse confici. Ego non video, quomodo peccatum illud actuale Adami, actio illa singularis magis nostra actio, nostrum peccatum fuerit, quam ejus persona fuit nostra persona. Si id vides, ostende quaeso mihi & explica: magnam tibi habebo gratiam.
latin.287: GAR. Huic ergo primae inobedientiae, non quidem praecise sumptae, sed una cum corruptione quam effecit in Adamo nobis imputatur, sicut supra vir doctus agnoscebat, erit sane etiam per eam imputationem nostra. Quidni ergo & Adami persona nobis imputetur, & dicatur etiam fuisse persona nostra? Aut hoc vir doctus concedat, aut suam argumentandi rationem condemnet & eliminet: & fateatur quod res est, nunquam auditum alienas personas imputari, sed actionum imputationem rem esse omnium ore atque sermone tritam, &c. PLAC. Quo sensu dixerim, & quam is minime causae quam ago obsit, actionem illam primam inobedientiae cum corruptione quam peperit nobis imputari, supra expositum est pag. 162. 163. Quod inde colligit, illam actionem etiam per eam imputationem nostram esse; non agnosco. Nam corruptio nostra est, quia in nos propagata est. Actio autem illa nostra fit non imputatione, sed, ut dicebat Lavaterus, vitio originis: quia nempe vitium originis seu corruptio est inobedientiae illius communicatio, & habitualis in eam consension: itaque non est nostra, quia nobis imputatur; sed contra nobis imputatur, quia nostra est.

pass_a.282: You add that this forces us to confess Adam's first sin was otherwise regarded, and by God's just judgment imputed and ascribed to all human nature. I would rather confess my ignorance—and not be ashamed of that confession. Blind is he who does not feel he is ignorant of far more than he knows. How many things in nature have reasons we cannot give for why they are so? Better that, in my view, than bursting into God's secret mind and ascribing to Him without any revelation a consideration and judgment that perhaps never was and does not become Him. You know Isaiah 55: my thoughts are not as your thoughts; as the heavens are high above the earth, so are my thoughts above yours—and who has known the mind of the Lord?
pass_a.283: GAR opens by saying he would rather take my stance as not the feigned ignorance Job 21:14 condemns—people telling God to leave and refusing knowledge of His ways—than nurse a dark view of the learned man. PLAC answers: which of my words invited that dark view? And how does a humble, devout refusal to go beyond Scripture resemble the wicked impiety of Job's criminals?
pass_a.284: GAR wonders why I treat seekers of original corruption's cause—and of birth-penalties on posterity—in first-sin imputation (and so participation) as invaders of God's hidden mind, when he knows ancients and moderns teach that and claim Romans 5 as their source, with many proofs still to come. Branding them all as rash trespassers of the Deuteronomy 29:29 bounds, he doubts, sits ill with fidelity. PLAC: The live issue was that inward divine act said to make God regard all as one man in Adam. Did the ancients and moderns assert that? Does Romans 5 yield it? Did he pile testimonies for it? To credit God with an unscriptural, irrational inward consideration of mind and will—if that is not storming the secret mind, what is?
pass_a.285: I allow the same charge could hit immediate imputation as the alleged cause of original corruption whenever it cannot be drawn from holy Writ—for that too is an inward divine act of mind and will. Loading me with bias and rousing theologians against me is wasted: I accuse none of them; I warn brothers, as a brother, to shun this shoal. Erring is human; clinging to error after a warning is base and perilous. Strange that Reformed teachers brandish against their own the very prejudices that most block truth, then and now. Our rule is not this doctor's or that one's lesson, but only what the one Teacher spoke by Apostles and Prophets. Scripture, most ancients, and some reputable moderns never taught that imputation—and he even cites some against his own case. Witness Lavater of Zurich (one sample): in his 2 Chronicles 25 commentary (quoted Cap. XVIII p. 629) each bears his own crimes' penalties, yet God is not tied to that law, for He justly punishes in all the first parents' sin as each one's own by origin's vice. That clashes hardest with the claim that their sin is ours only by imputation.
pass_a.286: Suppose I press you for why that first sin alone—here I am lost. You volunteer, unasked: because Adam was first man, origin, stock, root of all. From a root I can see vice traveling with nature into offspring; I will not grant that his actual deed was therefore ours or owed us as an imputed charge, nor that your ascribed divine consideration-and-judgment follows. How that singular act was more our act and sin than his person was our person I cannot see. If you can, demonstrate and unpack it—I will thank you greatly.
pass_a.287: GAR presses: the first disobedience, not bare but joined to the corruption it made in Adam, is charged to us (as I earlier allowed), and so becomes ours by that charging. Why not then charge Adam's person too and call it ours? Either concede that, or scrap the argument, and admit persons are never heard to be imputed—only actions, a commonplace on every tongue. PLAC: How I meant—and how little it wounds my case—that the first disobedience-act with the corruption it bred is charged to us, I already showed at pp. 162–163. From that he infers the act itself is ours by the charging; I refuse. Corruption is ours as propagated into us. The act is ours not by charging but, with Lavater, by origin's vice: that vice or corruption is the sharing of that disobedience and habitual consent to it. Hence it is not ours because charged; rather it is charged because it is already ours.

282: You subjoin that this compels us to confess that that first sin of Adam was considered in another way, and by God's just judgment imputed and ascribed to the whole human nature. I would rather confess my ignorance; nor would I be ashamed of this confession: for I judge him blind who does not feel that he is ignorant of far more than he knows. How many things there are in nature whose reasons why they happen so we cannot give? Better that, in my judgment, than bursting into God's secret mind and ascribing to Him without any revelation a consideration and judgment which perhaps neither was nor becomes Him. For you know that word of Isaiah 55: my thoughts are not as your thoughts. As the heavens are high above the earth, so high are my thoughts above your thoughts. And that: who has known the mind of the Lord?
283: GAR. Here indeed I also first profess that I prefer to believe that this is not the affected ignorance of which those speak in Job chapter 21 verse 14—'Depart from us; we do not want the knowledge of your ways'—rather than to foster some sinister opinion of the learned man. PLAC. What handle, I ask, did I give by those words for fostering a sinister opinion of me, or what is there in this modest and religious ignorance of mine, by which I refuse to be wise beyond Scripture, like to the abominable impiety of those criminals in Job?
284: GAR. I only marvel by what reason he judges that those who seek the cause of original corruption, and of all the penalties lying upon posterity from birth itself, in the imputation—and so the participation—of the first sin are bursting into God's secret mind, when he is not unaware that older and more recent theologians both teach this and profess that they drew it from the Apostle's doctrine in Romans 5, as will afterward be proved by most frequent testimonies. To press all these with so grave an accusation, as if by rash daring bursting into God's secret mind and crossing those limits which God set for man in Deuteronomy 29:29—I do not know whether it is sufficiently agreeable to faithfulness. PLAC. First the debate was about that inward act of God by which God was said to have considered all men as one man in Adam. Did the older and more recent theologians say that? Can that be gathered from the Apostle's doctrine in Romans 5? Did the learned man bring most frequent testimonies to prove it? To ascribe to God a consideration—a certain inward act of mind and will—beyond Scripture, beyond reason: what is it to burst into God's secret mind, if this is not?
285: The same, I confess, can be said of that immediate imputation in which the cause of original corruption is sought, if indeed it cannot be gathered from the sacred letters. For that too is an inward act of the divine mind and will. In vain he loads me with prejudices; in vain he stirs up the minds of theologians against me: for I do not accuse them, but brotherly warn them to beware this reef for themselves. For it is human to err, but to persist in error when warned is very shameful and dangerous. And I marvel that Reformed theologians use against their own brothers such prejudices as once, and in this time, have more than anything hindered the knowing of the truth. For not what this man or that taught is the rule of our faith, but only that which our one Teacher taught through His Apostles and Prophets. But that imputation neither Scripture, nor most of the older theologians, nor certain more recent ones of fair name taught: and some the learned man himself praises against himself. Let Ludovicus Lavater, the distinguished Zurich theologian, be an example (for to have brought one example will suffice in this place), whose these words from the Commentary on 2 Chronicles 25 he cites at Cap. XVIII, page 629: Let each pay the penalties of his own crimes. God is not bound by this law. For He justly punishes in all men the sin of the first parents, which by the vice of origin is each one's own. What can more oppose the doctrine of the learned man, who everywhere affirms that the sin of the first parents becomes ours only by imputation?
286: What if I ask of you the reason why that first— for it wholly escapes me. Although you seem of your own accord, unasked, to have wished to give a reason, for you add these words: because, namely, Adam was the first man, the origin and stock, or root, of all men. I acknowledge it; from this I understand that he could, together with human nature, propagate his vice into posterity: but I deny that therefore his actual sin was ours, or ought to have been imputed to us; I deny that from that the consideration and judgment which you ascribe to God can be made out. I do not see how that actual sin of Adam, that singular action, was more our action, our sin, than his person was our person. If you see that, show it to me, I beg, and explain: I will hold great gratitude to you.
287: GAR. To this first disobedience, then—not indeed taken precisely by itself, but together with the corruption which it effected in Adam—is imputed to us, as the learned man above acknowledged; it will indeed also be ours through that imputation. Why then should not Adam's person also be imputed to us, and be said also to have been our person? Let the learned man either grant this, or condemn and eliminate his way of arguing: and confess what the fact is—it was never heard that alien persons are imputed, but that the imputation of actions is a thing worn in everyone's mouth and speech, etc. PLAC. In what sense I said—and how little that hinders the cause I am pleading—that that first action of disobedience with the corruption which it bore is imputed to us, was set out above at pages 162–163. What he gathers from that, that that action is ours also through that imputation, I do not acknowledge. For the corruption is ours because it was propagated into us. But that action becomes ours not by imputation, but, as Lavater said, by the vice of origin: because of course the vice of origin or corruption is the communication of that disobedience, and a habitual consent to it; and so it is not ours because it is imputed to us; but on the contrary it is imputed to us because it is ours.
